Failing Sometimes

By Skyler Crossman

What's an emotional arc without some math?

Sometimes people make predictions about the future, and sometimes their predictions come true, other times they don't. One common tool for scoring predictions about the future- that is, figuring out who is generally more accurate- is called a Brier score. A basic version looks like this: shows Brier = (p-o)^2 on the projector where p is your prediction- you write it as a number between 0 and 1 like .75 for 75% - and o is the outcome, 0 or 1. A perfect Brier score is a score of 0.

Funny thing about the Brier score. It's basically impossible to get a perfect score. You'd have to know, 100%, what the answer would be. Since you aren't that sure, you're going to lose a few points with every guess. If you tried to guess and say you were 100% sure, you'd lose a lot of points when you wound up wrong. When dealing in prediction, 0 and 1 are not probabilities. Nobody is correctly 100% sure of anything.

So to make predictions is to set yourself up for a little bit of failure.

Some people fear failure.

Actually, that makes it sound very abstract. I personally am afraid of failing. When I was a kid and still learning to walk- I don't remember this personally, but it's been told to me by my parents- I would half crouch, clinging for support to various objects. It took a long time for me to walk fully upright, as though I was afraid of falling over. Not so my sibling, who at the same age would stand right up- and just as fast fall right back down. The same pattern repeated when we learned to surfboard. I hunched over almost the whole time, never letting my centre of gravity get too high, while my sibling stood upright almost as soon as they got the first wave, and went right off the board into the water.

When it doesn't matter, I can fail all day. Playing the guitar alone in my room, I'll make mistake after mistake and just try again. I learned to program computers via trial and error on a calculator, just typing instructions into the thing and watching what failed. I can even fail in front of people without fear if it's in a context where it doesn't matter; in high school I learned to play a videogame by losing repeatedly to a good friend of mine, over and over and over. But as soon as I contemplate playing guitar in front of people I don't know very well, I get scared. What if I play a wrong note? Do you feel more nervous to make a prediction in front of your boss who's about to write it down?

Sometimes it feels like my professional life needs to be an unbroken string of success. Get good grades in school, get a good internship with glowing reviews, get a good first job, move on from that job at the right time. If I get a bad review, or get fired, I worry that I'll have to settle for something less than I could have had at the next place.

This is the point of the speech where I tell some people that failure isn't as bad as they think. And indeed, it's generally fine to just fall off the surf board. You can just not mention that D in Calculus, or the terrible phone tech support job that only lasted a few months; nobody's asked my GPA in about a decade. I do habitually make predictions, and my average Brier score is about .2 these days. But some failures aren't going to be recovered from.

I have a boxer fracture. I've been studying martial arts since I was seven years old. I've wrapped my hands often enough to lose count, I've been told how to hold my wrist and what to be careful of. And then one day I spent three seconds not thinking about that, and now part of one hand looks wrong and doesn't move as smooth as the other side. I got lucky. I know other people who made one wrong move one day and now they don't have all their original teeth, or they're still wearing a back brace from downstream complications.

Sometimes a relationship breaks up, and you are never, ever getting back together again.

When I was considering what to do with my career, I considered medicine, then decided I didn't want to be regularly in situations where my mistake could cost someone their life. Instead, I went into software, on the assumption that obviously there was no way to make some accidental mistake writing code which would kill anybody.

So anyway, I make a lot of mistakes. Tracking your predictions is a sport for a certain kind of bravery.

So we have a lot of problems. We have so many problems, sorting them by which problems everyone is neglecting and what we have any traction on is a job all on its own. Some of those problems are so hard to solve, I am pretty sure I wouldn't understand a correct solution on a blueprint if you showed it to me.

And we can fail. I want you to understand that- I, I want to understand that. The laws of nature do not care. The Chartists never got their list of demands satisfied. People still die of stupid preventable industrial accidents, we die of fires and of plague and of car crashes and those are the problems that we basically know how to fix. Maybe in a hundred years we'll have answers for Parkinson's and Sarcopenia the way we now have answers for Scurvy but right now we don't.

Every human being who died under slavery is a tragedy that can never be undone. Some of us in this room would say that's true of every human being who has ever died, full stop. And we just keep dying, just a little faster than one person every other second. snap count to two snap count to two snap.

I don't know how to fix that. We just sang about doing the next right thing, but I don't know what the next right thing is. Maybe someone else does, but I don't know who. No rescuer hath the rescuer.

To make the world better, we're going to have to act under uncertainty. We need to take risks. There isn't another way to act. And. . . I'm afraid of that. I want to work on computers where I can back things up and test them exhaustively. Courage is the Hogwarts virtue I have the least of. And I wish we could all take as long as we needed to build up the courage to take that next step, but I don't think the world is going to wait for us, and I'm hoping that somebody here tonight is braver than I am-

-because I'm still here. Hanging out in the city where I've got friends, still in a job where nobody dies if I mess up. Getting more anxious by the year, accumulating fractures and aversions faster than I get over them. I keep thinking if I read more about the problems, if I make a few more friends in the field, accumulate a little more resources, then it will be the time to make a move.

Hesitation is always easy. Rarely useful.

There are so many dangers in the world. There's also so many heroes. We're not doomed, we just have a big todo list. Earlier I said "no rescuer hath the rescuer," but that's not true: if a firefighter falls, there are other firefighters to go pull them out of the burning building. There are so many heroes.

The Smallpox plague fell to Edward Jenner and Donald Henderson and others. Clair Patterson and Herbert Needleman sounded the alarm against the pollution of leaded gasoline. Norman Borlaug and Gurdev Khush struck an immense blow against famine with better wheat and rice. They may bury our bodies when we die, but we are not dead yet and as long as any human is left standing we're not going to stop trying to make things better, we are not resigned to the shutting away of loving hearts in the hard ground, we are not fucking going to let fear stop us from making tomorrow brighter than today, and I am 100% confident that some day every human being will grow up in health and safety, that humankind will last until the last lit sun fades to black. There are many scary things but you know what, world? Humankind is here and we're scarier, and I know we're going to win.

Someday when the descendants of humanity have spread from star to star, they won't tell the children about the history of ancient earth until they're old enough to bear it; and when they learn they'll weep to hear that such a thing as Death had ever once existed.

I know that we will make tomorrow brighter than today.
